lead: A recurrent network that predicts the next word is the engine behind three headline tasks. Language modelling learns the probability of a sentence. Translation reads one sequence and writes another. Image captioning turns a picture into a short sentence. The core loop is identical in all three: keep a hidden state, produce a probability over the vocabulary, score or pick the next token. Only the encoder that fills the first state and the head that reads it change. That is why one unit covers all of them.
prereq: You need: the RNN hidden state, encoder-decoder models, word embeddings, and CNN feature vectors from Unit 3.

sections.h3: Language modelling: chain rule, cross-entropy, perplexity

blocks.text: A language model gives a probability to every sentence. Storing one number per sentence is impossible, so the sentence is broken into next-word predictions with the chain rule of probability.
P(w<sub>1</sub>, w<sub>2</sub>, …, w<sub>T</sub>) = ∏<sub>t=1</sub><sup>T</sup> P(w<sub>t</sub> | w<sub>1</sub>, …, w<sub>t−1</sub>)
blocks.where: w<sub>t</sub> is the token at position t; T is the number of tokens; P(w<sub>t</sub> | w<sub>1</sub>…w<sub>t−1</sub>) is the softmax probability the model gives to the true token at step t.

blocks.text: An RNN computes each factor. The embedding of the previous word and the previous hidden state give the new hidden state h<sub>t</sub>. A softmax over the vocabulary V turns h<sub>t</sub> into a probability for every possible next word. In training the true previous words are fed in (teacher forcing) and the loss is taken on the correct next word.
L = −(1/T) Σ<sub>t=1</sub><sup>T</sup> ln P(w<sub>t</sub> | w<sub>1</sub>…w<sub>t−1</sub>),   perplexity = exp(L)
blocks.where: L is the average negative log-likelihood per token, in nats; ln is the natural logarithm; exp(L) = e<sup>L</sup>; perplexity is the effective number of equally likely words the model is choosing between.

blocks.text: Lower perplexity is better. A model that puts probability 1 on every true word has L = 0 and perplexity 1. A perplexity of 3 means the model is as unsure as a fair guess among 3 words. The same model sits inside phone keyboard suggestions, speech-recognition rescoring, and the decoder half of a translator.

In translation the input and output are different sequences, often of different lengths. The encoder-decoder from 4.5 handles this. An encoder LSTM reads the source sentence into a context vector c. A decoder LSTM starts from c and emits target words until an end-of-sentence token appears.

blocks.where: x<sub>1</sub>…x<sub>N</sub> is the source sentence of length N; y<sub>1</sub>…y<sub>M</sub> is the target of length M; c is the encoder's context vector; each factor is one decoder softmax.

blocks.text: Training uses the same per-token cross-entropy as language modelling. At test time the true previous target is unknown, so the decoder feeds back its own last output. Small errors can then push the state away from anything seen in training.

BLEU scores a generated sentence against one or more human references. It counts matching n-grams (single words, pairs, triples), takes precision for each order, combines the orders with a geometric mean, and applies a brevity penalty so a short, safe output cannot win. BLEU lies between 0 and 1, and higher is better. It is an evaluation metric, not the loss you train on.

Sequence labelling is the many-to-many case: part-of-speech tagging and named-entity recognition read T words and emit T tags. The recurrent stack is unchanged. Only the head changes, to a per-step softmax over the tag set.

A picture is not a sequence; a caption is. The bridge is a CNN from Unit 3. A pretrained network such as VGG or ResNet reads the image and outputs a fixed feature vector v of a few hundred to a couple of thousand numbers. The decoder RNN takes v as its first input and then generates words one step at a time.
x<sub>0</sub> = W<sub>v</sub>v + b<sub>v</sub>,   h<sub>t</sub> = tanh(W<sub>h</sub>h<sub>t−1</sub> + W<sub>x</sub>x<sub>t</sub> + b),   P(w<sub>t</sub>) = softmax(W<sub>o</sub>h<sub>t</sub>)
blocks.where: v is the CNN feature vector; W<sub>v</sub> projects it to the RNN input size; x<sub>t</sub> is the embedding of the previous word for t ≥ 1; h<sub>t</sub> is the hidden state; W<sub>o</sub> maps the state to one score per vocabulary word.

blocks.text: Everything else is a language model. Training pairs each image with its human caption and minimises the per-word cross-entropy. At test time the decoder starts from v and a start token, picks the most likely word (greedy) or keeps a few candidate sentences alive (beam search), and stops at the end token. BLEU is also used to score captions against references.

Why a feature and not raw pixels: a 224×224 colour image is 150,528 input numbers, most of them redundant. A CNN vector of about 512 numbers already encodes objects and scene. The decoder then only has to learn language.

sections.h3: Video and time series: the advanced end

blocks.text: A video is a sequence of frames, so the captioning recipe extends to it. Run a CNN on each frame or clip and feed the frame features to an RNN that outputs an action label. Adding time inside the convolution gives 3D CNNs and two-stream models that see appearance and motion separately. Only a few universities teach these spatio-temporal models in detail. The same many-to-one RNN forecasts sensor time series, such as hourly electricity load or daily UPI transaction counts.

examples.question: An RNN language model scores the sentence 'the cat sat' as follows: P(the) = 0.5 at step 1, P(cat | the) = 0.4 at step 2, and P(sat | the cat) = 0.2 at step 3. The sentence ends after 'sat'. (a) Find the probability of the whole sentence. (b) Find the average cross-entropy loss in nats per token. (c) Find the perplexity. Use natural logarithms.
steps: Chain rule: P(the cat sat) = P(the) × P(cat | the) × P(sat | the cat) = 0.5 × 0.4 × 0.2.
Multiply: 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.20; then 0.20 × 0.2 = 0.04. So the sentence probability is 0.04, that is 4%.
Take natural logs: ln 0.5 = −0.6931, ln 0.4 = −0.9163, ln 0.2 = −1.6094. Their sum is −3.2189 nats.
Average negative log-likelihood: L = 3.2189 / 3 = 1.0730 nats per token.
examples.answer: Sentence probability P = 0.04 (4%), average loss L = 1.073 nats per token, and perplexity = 2.92.
examples.check:
import math
p1, p2, p3 = 0.5, 0.4, 0.2
P = p1 * p2 * p3
L = -(math.log(p1) + math.log(p2) + math.log(p3)) / 3
ppl = math.exp(L)
print(round(P, 4))
print(round(L, 4))
print(round(ppl, 2))

traps: Perplexity is exp of the average negative log-likelihood, not the product of probabilities. For the worked example, 25 = 1/0.04 is the reciprocal probability; 25^(1/3) = 2.92 is the perplexity.
Lower perplexity is better. A perplexity of 1 is a perfect model, and perplexity cannot be compared across models that use different tokenizers or vocabulary sizes.
Image captioning feeds a CNN feature vector into the decoder, never raw pixels. The CNN is the encoder; the RNN only writes words.
Teacher forcing is a training trick: the true previous word is supplied. At inference the model eats its own output, so the two settings are not the same.
BLEU is an evaluation metric, not the training loss, and a higher BLEU is better. The brevity penalty exists so that a short output with few words cannot get high precision for free.

quiz.q: State the chain rule that a language model uses to score a sentence of T tokens.
quiz.a: P(w<sub>1</sub>…w<sub>T</sub>) = ∏ P(w<sub>t</sub> | w<sub>1</sub>…w<sub>t−1</sub>). Each factor is a next-word probability produced by the softmax at step t.

quiz.q: Define perplexity and say whether a lower or higher value is better.
quiz.a: Perplexity = exp(L), where L is the average negative log-likelihood per token in nats. It is the effective number of equally likely words the model is choosing among. Lower is better; 1 is perfect.

quiz.q: Why does an image captioning model pass a CNN feature vector to the decoder instead of raw pixels?
quiz.a: Raw pixels for a 224×224 colour image are 150,528 numbers and mostly redundant. The CNN compresses them to a few hundred numbers that already encode objects and scene. The decoder then only learns language, which trains faster and generalises better.

quiz.q: Why does BLEU include a brevity penalty on top of n-gram precision?
quiz.a: Precision alone rewards very short outputs, because one correct word out of one gives precision 1. The brevity penalty shrinks the score when the output is much shorter than the reference, so recall matters too.

quiz.q: A model gives P(a) = 0.8, P(b | a) = 0.5 and P(c | a b) = 0.5, and the sentence ends after c. Find the sentence probability and the perplexity.
A translator is trained with teacher forcing but used without it. Explain the mismatch and give one visible symptom.
quiz.a: In training the decoder always receives the correct previous word, so it never learns to recover from its own errors. At test time it conditions on its own output, and one wrong word moves the hidden state off the training distribution. Symptom: the first words look fine and the sentence then degrades, drifts or repeats.

quiz.q: Model A has perplexity 20 and model B has 18 on the same test text. Which is better, and why can two models with different vocabularies not be compared by perplexity?
quiz.a: B is better, because lower perplexity means a higher average probability per token. Perplexity is defined per token; if the tokenizers or vocabulary sizes differ, the same text becomes a different number of tokens, so the numbers sit on different scales and cannot be compared.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production systems now replace the RNN with attention and transformers (Unit 5), but the objective on this page — per-token cross-entropy over a softmax — is unchanged. Image captioning has moved to transformer decoders that attend to many patch features instead of one fixed vector.
